verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.117, chapter 10 GENERAL ORGANIC CHEMISTRY, LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS question 30. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. The book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty. A MISMATCH IN THE SOURCE, HANDLED DELIBERATELY: the question asks for the classification of HYDROCARBONS, while the heading over the printed answer says classification of organic compounds based on the carbon skeleton. Those are not the same set. A hydrocarbon contains carbon and hydrogen only, so a heterocyclic ring — which contains nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur besides carbon — is not a hydrocarbon at all. This card answers the question that was asked, uses the same tree as its framework, and closes by naming the heterocyclic branch and saying plainly why it falls outside. A student who copies the whole organic-compound tree is not writing anything false about organic compounds; this card simply does not present heterocyclic compounds as hydrocarbons. CARRIED AS EXTRA CONTENT, not from the source book: the general formulae CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, CₙH₂ₙ and CₙH₂ₙ₋₂, Huckel's (4n + 2) rule quoted in the aromatic step, and azulene C₁₀H₈ as the non-benzenoid example. All are standard NCERT-level content and a teacher should confirm they are wanted at eight marks. NO FIGURE: this chapter's cards carry no figure objects, so the tree is written as named branches in order rather than drawn. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: Hydrocarbons and the first division
lines: A hydrocarbon is a compound made of
carbon and hydrogen only.
Hydrocarbons are classified first by the
shape of the carbon skeleton, which
gives two branches.
Open chain, also called acyclic: the
carbon atoms form a chain, straight or
branched, and there is no ring. These
are also called aliphatic compounds.
Closed chain, also called cyclic: the
carbon atoms form a ring.
steps.why: A long answer that is a classification needs its top-level split on the page before any example, because everything after it is a subdivision of one branch or the other. Defining the word hydrocarbon first also fixes the boundary of the whole answer, which the last step returns to.
common_mistakes: Starting with alkanes and alkenes. Those are two boxes inside the open chain branch, so the two branches have to be named first.
Including a compound that contains oxygen or nitrogen. A hydrocarbon is made of carbon and hydrogen only.
steps.memory_tip: Two branches first: no ring is open chain, a ring is closed chain.
steps.margin_note: Write the split before any example; everything after it belongs to one of these two branches.

steps.label: Open chain hydrocarbons
lines: Open chain hydrocarbons are saturated or
unsaturated.
Saturated — the alkanes. Every carbon to
carbon bond is a single bond.
Examples: ethane C₂H₆, propane C₃H₈ and
the branched 2-methylpropane C₄H₁₀.
Unsaturated — the alkenes. There is at
least one carbon to carbon double bond.
Examples: ethene CH₂=CH₂ and propene
CH₃–CH=CH₂.
Unsaturated — the alkynes. There is at
least one carbon to carbon triple bond.
Examples: ethyne HC≡CH and propyne
CH₃–C≡CH.
steps.why: The open chain branch carries two marks here because it covers three families, and each family is fixed by three things: the kind of bond, the general formula, and an example. Writing all three every time makes the three families comparable line by line instead of being three separate paragraphs.
common_mistakes: Giving the alkene formula as CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. That is the alkane formula; an alkene with one double bond is CₙH₂ₙ.
Putting branched chain compounds in a branch of their own. A branched chain still has no ring, so 2-methylpropane is an open chain alkane.
Calling an alkene saturated. Among the open chain families only the alkanes are saturated; a double or triple bond makes a hydrocarbon unsaturated.
steps.memory_tip: Single, double, triple bond: alkane, alkene, alkyne, and the formula drops by two hydrogen atoms each time.
steps.margin_note: Give bond, formula and example for each family; the three lines repeat in the same order.

steps.label: Closed chain hydrocarbons
lines: In a closed chain hydrocarbon the ring
is built of carbon atoms only, because a
hydrocarbon contains no other element.
Such a ring is called homocyclic, or
carbocyclic. Every cyclic hydrocarbon is
of this kind.
Homocyclic compounds are of two kinds:
alicyclic and aromatic.
steps.why: This step is short because it does one job: it names the branch that every cyclic hydrocarbon belongs to and splits it in two. Saying why the ring must be all carbon also prepares the closing step, where the branch that is not all carbon is named and set aside.
common_mistakes: Writing that a cyclic hydrocarbon may be homocyclic or heterocyclic. A heterocyclic ring contains nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur, so it is not a hydrocarbon.
Using the word homocyclic for an open chain compound. The word describes a ring built of one kind of atom.
steps.memory_tip: Homo means the same, so a homocyclic ring is carbon all the way round.
steps.margin_note: Name both kinds here; the next two steps take one each.

steps.label: Alicyclic hydrocarbons
lines: Alicyclic hydrocarbons are rings that
behave like the open chain compounds.
The saturated ones are the cycloalkanes,
in which every ring bond is single.
Examples: cyclopropane C₃H₆, cyclobutane
C₄H₈ and cyclohexane C₆H₁₂.
A ring may also be unsaturated, as in
cyclohexene C₆H₁₀, which has one double
bond in the ring.
steps.why: The alicyclic box is where a student sees that the ring and the chain families run in parallel: a cycloalkane is an alkane bent into a ring, and its formula is the alkene formula because closing the ring costs the same two hydrogen atoms a double bond does.
common_mistakes: Giving cyclohexane the formula C₆H₁₄. Closing the ring removes two hydrogen atoms, so cyclohexane is C₆H₁₂.
Calling every ring aromatic. A ring is aromatic only if it is planar and has delocalised π electrons; cyclohexane is not.
steps.memory_tip: A cycloalkane shares its formula with the alkenes: closing a ring costs two hydrogen atoms.
steps.margin_note: Give the ring formula here; it is the line that separates a cycloalkane from an alkane.

steps.label: Aromatic hydrocarbons
lines: Aromatic hydrocarbons have a planar ring
in which the π electrons are delocalised
over the whole ring.
n is a whole number 0, 1, 2 … Benzene
has six π electrons, so n = 1.
Aromatic hydrocarbons are of two kinds.
Benzenoid: the molecule contains one or
more benzene rings.
Examples: benzene C₆H₆, toluene
C₆H₅–CH₃, and naphthalene C₁₀H₈, which
is two benzene rings sharing an edge.
Non-benzenoid: the molecule is aromatic
but has no benzene ring in it.
Example: azulene C₁₀H₈, built from a
five-membered and a seven-membered ring
joined along one bond.
steps.why: Aromatic character is a property of the electrons, not of a particular ring size, so the rule is written before the examples. That order is what makes the non-benzenoid box possible to explain at all: azulene has no six-membered benzene ring, and it is still aromatic because it satisfies the same electron count.
common_mistakes: Writing that every aromatic hydrocarbon contains a benzene ring. The non-benzenoid compounds are aromatic without one.
Giving Huckel's rule as 4n π electrons. It is (4n + 2) π electrons, which is six for benzene.
Putting naphthalene among the non-benzenoid compounds. It is built of two benzene rings, so it is benzenoid.
steps.memory_tip: Aromatic means flat with (4n + 2) delocalised π electrons; benzene has six, so n = 1.
steps.margin_note: Write Huckel's rule before the two boxes; it is what the word aromatic means.

steps.label: Rings with another element

lines.text: Only carbon and hydrogen, in every branch

lines: The wider classification of organic
compounds by carbon skeleton adds one
more branch on the cyclic side:
heterocyclic compounds, whose ring
contains nitrogen, oxygen or sulphur
besides carbon, and which are aromatic
or non-aromatic.
Those compounds contain an element
other than carbon and hydrogen, so they
are not hydrocarbons and fall outside
this classification.
steps.why: The question is about hydrocarbons, and the tree a student has usually seen drawn is the wider one for organic compounds, which carries a heterocyclic branch. Naming that branch and saying in one line why it falls outside is what keeps the answer to the question asked without leaving a reader wondering where the missing box went.
common_mistakes: Listing pyridine or furan as cyclic hydrocarbons. Their rings contain nitrogen and oxygen, so they are heterocyclic compounds and not hydrocarbons.
Leaving the heterocyclic branch out with no comment. Naming it and saying why it is excluded shows the boundary of the classification.
steps.memory_tip: If the ring contains anything but carbon, the compound is not a hydrocarbon.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming the boundary of the classification completes the answer.

insider_note: This is a tree, so the answer is easiest to read when it works down the branches in order rather than as a list of families. Starting from open chain and closed chain, and giving one general formula and one named example in every box, is a comfortable length for eight marks.
